Supply Chain & Custody

The Screen Was Listening: Cellular Implants Inside Resold Ledgers

Where the foam padding behind a Ledger Nano X screen should sit, tampered units bought through a Southeast Asian reseller carried a scraped microcontroller, a cellular modem and a custom antenna wired straight into the display lines.

By the Hardware & Security Desk · Ungovernable · HRF · Bitcoin Magazine

A cryptographic attestation check can prove that a secure element is genuine, and still say nothing about what is reading the screen over its shoulder. Across Thursday and Friday, engineers and freedom-tech researchers dissected a hardware supply-chain attack against Ledger Nano X devices acquired through a reseller in Southeast Asia, in which organized criminals replaced internal foam with an independent radio transmitter.

Ungovernable laid out the anatomy of the implant in detail: Where the foam padding behind a Ledger Nano X screen should be: a microcontroller with its markings scraped off, a Nordic cellular modem, an eSIM and a custom antenna. It's wired into the lines that carry data to the screen. When setup shows your 24 words, it reads them and sends them to the attacker over its own mobile connection.

Because the tap sits on the display bus rather than inside the enclave, the cryptographic handshake with the host software proceeds normally. It never goes near the secure chip, so the device passes the genuine check. Ledger's own docs say the check can't detect this. Ungovernable noted. In its 142nd Financial Freedom Report, the Human Rights Foundation (HRF) confirmed that the tampered devices were sold through a Southeast Asian reseller and noted that an on-chain investigator estimates losses above $86 million, while Ungovernable's brief put the drained total at $93 million.

The lesson echoed a line Fedi posted from Imagine IF earlier in the window: A customer list is a target list — the only list that doesn't leak is the one you never collect. And elsewhere on the security beat, Marcel and Nate marked a passage from a Malwarebytes report on how a single credential opened nearly nine million personal records: A weak, leaked password opened an authorized route into a sensitive register. That access allowed millions of searches, and the activity was discovered only after an unusually large bill drew attention to it. As Nate's second highlight noted, TV 2 says an email containing the password 123456 had appeared in a larger data leak—while Mr.Crown // Renarchy pointed to 6.39 million personal records compromised in an earlier Odido breach.

Ungovernable

From the prison beat, Ungovernable published the seventh letter from Samourai Wallet developer Keonne Rodriguez after his transfer out of Morgantown, capturing the sensory reality of federal detention in four short lines:

11PM. Keonne asks his cellmate what time they turn the lights off. They don't. He covers his head with a sheet that smells of motor oil and sawdust, lies with half his body on bare metal, and asks himself if a year off his sentence was worth leaving Morgantown. Protocol Architecture

The Outbox Model Proves Its Speed as Clients Debate Microapps

Canoe and Applesauce show that reading from authors' declared write relays works in seconds—while fiatjaf, hodlbod and hzrd149 hash out the boundary between napps and sandboxed napplets.

By the Protocol Desk · hodlbod · hzrd149 · fiatjaf

hodlbod released Canoe (gitea.coracle.social/coracle/canoe), a personal relay designed to end home-relay fragmentation by pulling an author's own notes from their declared NIP-65 outbox relays rather than scraping a web of trust. Even better, if you run two instances they will actively copy your notes between them without any configuration other than a normal 10002. Use the outbox model. It works. hodlbod wrote.

Hours later, hzrd149 backed that claim with benchmark numbers from the upcoming release of Applesauce: More sync tests from the upcoming version of applesauce, first one tries to connect to all my contacts relays ( 165 ) and gets ~1900 events in 34s. the second connects to the 30 most common and gets ~1700 events in 18s. Meanwhile, Cody argued that It's time for clients to let relays handle building the following feed. and opened iOS public testing on TestFlight for PsstPsst (s99).

On the application layer, fiatjaf shipped Verdana on Zapstore—a launcher for small HTML or raw WASM microapps ("napps") that pass messages to one another—warning on the timeline that Many bugs, but that's because Android is awful. Will fix, but try Verdana on the desktop if you are truly wise (s277). hodlbod asked whether "napplets" could be parameterized inside Flotilla with relay or room arguments, prompting hzrd149 to draw the security boundary between the two approaches: worth also pointing out the biggest difference is napps are default sites so they can access the full internet. napplets are heavily sandboxed so what they are allowed to do is completely controlled by the app they are running inside of.

Cryptography, Agents & Circular Economies

Encrypted Group Messaging

Marmot, Cordn and NIP-17 on a 240 MHz ESP32 Badge

Max · s548 · cloud fodder · Richard Nakamoto

Private group messaging over Nostr advanced on three fronts at once. Max published two technical deep dives into the Marmot Protocol (MLS over Nostr, MIP-00 through MIP-06), explaining how MIP-06 handles multi-device membership (s548): MIP-06 gives each device its own MLS key material and its own leaf in the ratchet tree. Every leaf carries the same Nostr pubkey in the credential identity field. The devices share an identity but share no cryptographic state, which means compromising one device does not hand the attacker the keys to the other.

In the app catalog, cloud fodder shipped Staircase, an end-to-end encrypted MLS group messenger built on Cordn (RFC 9420) with multi-device linking and Amber signing. And for constrained hardware, Richard Nakamoto demonstrated that an ESP32 microcontroller running MicroPythonOS (240 MHz, 8 MB PSRAM) already holds 80% of the code needed for NIP-17 encrypted group chat rooms.

Juraj🏴💛🌘 · routstr · evacide

Juraj🏴💛🌘 released Localhost Recording Studio, an open-source app running the YuE2-3B model directly on Android, macOS and Linux to generate full stereo songs offline:

The zombie apocalypse started on a Tuesday. You're alone in a forest, running, and the cell towers went down on day one. It should feel like a movie. It doesn't, and it takes you a minute to see why: there's no soundtrack, just your breathing. So you pull out your phone, open Localhost Recording Studio and make one. Run, run, run.

Essays & Reflections

When You're Paid in Stones, Weighing Physics by the Kilo, and Letting Kloak Go

omarvgws · Michael Meyen · Alex Gleason · Daryn Cavalier

Writing from Avalon Tulum in When You're Paid in Stones (s563), omarvgws reflected on receiving a third incomplete bank transfer in a melting currency: A payment that arrives the way dirty water arrives through a broken pipe: enough to survive by, too little to feel that someone, on the other side, honours the agreement. He contrasted fiat stones with the seeds of a circular economy: Can I pay someone in stones, when I ought to have paid in seeds?

In German long-form (s573), Michael Meyen reviewed six autumn books by putting them on the kitchen scale first—led at a full kilogram by Jochen Kirchhoff's Antigeschichte der Physik, published by Hauke Ritz's new imprint Hirschmann. And in the highlights desk, Alex Gleason marked a farewell passage from the Kloak team (kloak.app): But it’s time to let this go now. Not because it wasn’t worth it, but because we’ve given it everything we had, and there isn’t any more to give. Meanwhile, Daryn Cavalier highlighted page 168 of Biological Elegance: Unwitting the Devil: If we are to preserve any useful meaning to the word, consciousness has to be experiential. It can only come from within a finite system that is experiencing an infinite reality.
